This attack leverages the shared vulnerabilities across architectures or training styles. It demonstrates the lack of true diversity in many AI systems and exposes systemic risks.
Cross-Model Transferability
Cross-model transferability is the tendency of adversarial examples or poisoned data to impact multiple different models, even those trained independently. High transferability means that an attack doesn't need full access to the target model to succeed. This phenomenon complicates black-box defense and underscores the challenge of securing shared ecosystems.
Crowdsourced Labeling Exploit
A crowdsourced labeling exploit takes advantage of weaknesses in human-in-the-loop data labeling platforms. Attackers may intentionally inject mislabeled or misleading examples during open annotation campaigns. These corrupted labels subtly degrade model quality or embed strategic errors, especially in systems that rely on weak supervision or minimal post-label validation.
Data Camouflage
Data camouflage refers to the practice of hiding poisoned or adversarial samples within benign-looking data so they bypass quality checks and filtering. This technique is used to insert harmful examples during training without drawing attention. It often relies on imperceptible noise, ambiguous labeling, or stylistic blending to avoid detection.
Data Drift
Data drift refers to a gradual change in the statistical properties of input data over time, which can lead to degraded model performance. This shift may be caused by changes in user behavior, environments, or adversarial influence. Detecting and correcting for data drift is essential to maintaining reliable predictions in deployed systems.
Data Memorization
Data memorization occurs when a model retains and reproduces specific examples from its training data, sometimes including personally identifiable or sensitive content. This is particularly problematic in large models trained on unfiltered datasets. Attackers can exploit memorization to extract training data or trigger unintended disclosures.
Data Poisoning
Data poisoning is an adversarial attack that introduces maliciously crafted samples into the training set, causing the model to learn incorrect or biased behaviors. Poisoning can lead to misclassifications, backdoors, or broader system degradation. It is one of the most challenging and stealthy threats in machine learning security.
Decision Boundary
A decision boundary is the surface or region in input space where a model switches from one prediction to another. Understanding this boundary is critical to identifying where the model is most vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Attackers often aim to push inputs across decision boundaries with minimal changes.
Decision-Boundary Probing
Decision-boundary probing involves methodically testing inputs near a model's classification threshold to learn its internal structure or weaknesses. This technique can be used to reverse-engineer decision logic or craft high-confidence adversarial examples. It's often employed in black-box model extraction and boundary-based evasion attacks.
Deferred Trigger
A deferred trigger is a backdoor or adversarial mechanism that only activates after a series of interactions or time-based conditions. Unlike immediate triggers, deferred triggers are harder to detect through static analysis or simple red-teaming. They are useful for delayed exploitation in long-running systems or agent-based environments.
Embedding Consistency Checks
Embedding consistency checks are techniques used to verify that the internal representations (embeddings) of similar inputs remain stable across model versions or inputs. These checks help detect model drift, fine-tuning contamination, or adversarial interference. Significant deviations may signal underlying vulnerabilities or intentional manipulation.
Embedding Drift
Embedding drift occurs when the vector representations of similar inputs begin to diverge over time or across models. This drift may be caused by model updates, data changes, or adversarial fine-tuning. It can affect search, retrieval, and reasoning systems that rely on stable semantic representations.
Embedding Drift Conditioning
Embedding drift conditioning is an adversarial method where inputs are crafted to gradually shift a model's embedding space over time. By exploiting drift, attackers can influence similarity-based systems or downstream applications. It represents a long-game approach to corrupting model behavior without immediate detection.
Embedding Fragility
Embedding fragility refers to the sensitivity of learned vector representations to minor input changes, making them susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Fragile embeddings can lead to sharp shifts in downstream predictions or behavior. Securing embedding spaces is crucial for robust classification, clustering, and semantic matching.
Embedding Layer
The embedding layer is the part of a neural network that transforms discrete input elements—such as words, tokens, or items—into continuous vector representations. It serves as the model's initial perception of the input space and plays a critical role in downstream reasoning. Because of its foundational role, it's a frequent target for adversarial attacks aiming to manipulate semantic understanding.
Embedding Sensitivity
Embedding sensitivity refers to how much the embedding vector of an input changes in response to small perturbations or edits. High sensitivity can indicate vulnerability to adversarial examples or instability in downstream performance. Monitoring and minimizing this sensitivity is a common strategy in robust model design.
Embedding Similarity
Embedding similarity is a measure of how closely two inputs are represented within a model's learned vector space, often calculated using cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. It underpins many tasks like nearest-neighbor search, semantic matching, and content retrieval. Attackers may exploit similarity scores to evade filters or inject deceptive content.
Embedding Space
The embedding space is the multi-dimensional vector space where input features—such as words, images, or audio—are represented as continuous vectors. Models use this space to reason about semantic relationships. When compromised, the embedding space can act as a conduit for model confusion, misclassification, or unwanted behavior generalization.
Embedding Space Manipulation
Embedding space manipulation refers to adversarial techniques that deliberately shift or reshape the model's learned representations. This can be used to forge semantic similarities, alter model reasoning, or hide malicious content behind benign-looking vectors. Such manipulation is particularly dangerous in retrieval-augmented generation and zero-shot classification.
Embedding Space Perturbation
Embedding space perturbation involves small, targeted changes to a model's learned representations that result in downstream effects like misranking, misclassification, or semantic confusion. These perturbations are often designed to evade detection while degrading model performance. They highlight the fragility of vector-based reasoning in many AI systems.
Embedding-Space Constraint
An embedding-space constraint is a formal or informal rule applied to ensure the structure or relationships within the vector space remain valid and meaningful. Constraints may include distance thresholds, clustering behavior, or projection bounds. They are used both in defense design and adversarial training to enforce stability and interpretability.
Embedding-Space Drift
Embedding-space drift is a gradual change in the global structure or internal consistency of a model's learned vector space, often due to training updates, adversarial fine-tuning, or shifting data. This drift can lead to unpredictable or incoherent outputs in systems that rely on semantic similarity. Monitoring embedding-space stability is essential in long-lived or continually updated models.
Emergent Behavior
Emergent behavior refers to complex, often unexpected patterns of model performance or reasoning that arise from training large models at scale. These behaviors are not explicitly programmed but appear as side effects of architecture, data, and optimization dynamics. While sometimes beneficial, emergent behaviors also create new attack surfaces and interpretability challenges.
Empirical Robustness Curve
An empirical robustness curve is a graph showing how a model's accuracy or performance degrades as input perturbations increase. It is used to visualize the model's resistance to adversarial attacks or noise. Analysts and defenders use this curve to benchmark robustness and compare different models or defense strategies.
Entry Point
An entry point is the location or mechanism through which inputs are introduced into an AI system—such as a user interface, API call, or data pipeline. It represents a potential attack surface where adversaries can inject manipulated content, prompts, or code. Securing entry points is a foundational aspect of adversarial defense and system hardening.
Environmental State Manipulation
Environmental state manipulation involves altering the context or environment in which an AI system operates in order to influence its behavior. This is especially relevant in robotics, agentic AI, and reinforcement learning settings. Adversaries can use this method to mislead the model about its surroundings or goals, resulting in degraded or dangerous outcomes.
Ethical Constraint Mechanism
An ethical constraint mechanism is a built-in rule or control that restricts an AI system from performing actions considered harmful, unethical, or non-compliant. These mechanisms may rely on logic-based rules, safety classifiers, or policy filters. Attackers often attempt to bypass these constraints using prompt injection, adversarial inputs, or misdirection.
Expectation-over-Transformation
Expectation-over-transformation (EoT) is a defense method that evaluates a model's output across a range of transformed inputs—such as rotated, resized, or translated versions—to assess stability. By averaging predictions over these variants, models can resist small, adversarial changes. EoT is widely used in vision systems and certifiable defense strategies.
Experience Replay Buffer
An experience replay buffer is a memory structure used in reinforcement learning systems to store and reuse past interactions. It helps models learn more efficiently by sampling from diverse experiences. If compromised, attackers can poison the buffer with misleading or adversarial experiences, causing the agent to learn harmful behaviors.
Explanation Regularization
Explanation regularization is a training strategy that penalizes models for producing poor or misleading explanations for their predictions. It encourages models to align their internal reasoning with human-interpretable logic or ground truth concepts. This technique improves transparency and can offer some resilience against adversarial manipulation of attention or feature attribution.
External Execution Layer
An external execution layer refers to a part of an AI system that interacts with tools, APIs, or external environments beyond the model's internal logic. In agentic or multi-modal systems, this layer carries out real-world actions such as API calls, web queries, or file operations. Vulnerabilities here can allow attackers to hijack behavior or induce unintended consequences via manipulated inputs.
Fallback Execution Paths
Fallback execution paths are alternative behaviors or routines that an AI system uses when primary operations fail or yield uncertain results. These paths are often included to improve robustness or maintain continuity of service. However, if not carefully secured, they can be manipulated by adversaries to bypass controls or introduce harmful logic.
Feature Collision
Feature collision occurs when different inputs map to similar feature representations within a model's internal layers, often leading to incorrect or confused predictions. Attackers can exploit this by crafting adversarial examples that mimic the internal signature of benign inputs. It's a core tactic in evasion and backdoor attacks.
Federated Aggregation
Federated aggregation is the process of combining model updates from multiple decentralized clients in a federated learning system. It allows for collaborative model training without sharing raw data. Attackers may attempt to poison individual updates or exploit the aggregation function itself to introduce model-wide vulnerabilities.
Federated Learning
Federated learning is a decentralized training method where models are trained across multiple devices or nodes without centralizing the data. Each participant updates the model locally, and only the model updates are aggregated. While privacy-preserving, this setup introduces new risks such as update poisoning, client impersonation, and gradient leakage.
Feedback Loop Exploitation
Feedback loop exploitation occurs when an attacker manipulates an AI system's outputs or environment to gradually influence its future behavior. This is common in recommendation systems, social platforms, or autonomous agents that retrain on their own outputs. Adversaries can exploit this loop to reinforce bias, amplify misinformation, or degrade model performance over time.
Fine-Tuning
Fine-tuning is the process of taking a pre-trained model and continuing its training on a smaller, task-specific dataset to adapt it to a particular use case. It enables faster development and better performance on niche tasks. However, it can also be exploited to inject adversarial behavior or backdoors into otherwise trusted models.
Fine-Tuning Compromise
Fine-tuning compromise refers to the malicious modification of a model during the fine-tuning phase, often to introduce backdoors or trigger misbehavior under specific conditions. These attacks are hard to detect because they don't typically degrade performance on test data. Supply chain risks increase when using third-party or community-contributed fine-tuned models.
Fine-Tuning Contamination
Fine-tuning contamination occurs when the data used to fine-tune a model includes poisoned, biased, or otherwise untrustworthy examples. This contamination may be accidental or deliberate and can result in undesirable emergent behaviors, reduced generalization, or hidden vulnerabilities. Screening fine-tuning datasets is essential for model integrity.
Fine-Tuning Memorization
Fine-tuning memorization describes the phenomenon where a model learns to reproduce specific examples from its fine-tuning set, sometimes verbatim. This risk is amplified in small data settings and can lead to privacy violations or copyright issues. Attackers may exploit memorization to extract sensitive training data via probing.
Fine-Tuning Pipeline
The fine-tuning pipeline includes the processes, tools, and data involved in adapting a pre-trained model to a specialized task. It often integrates dataset preparation, training orchestration, checkpoint handling, and deployment. Each stage presents opportunities for compromise, especially when using automated workflows or externally sourced resources.
Formal Verification
Formal verification is the use of mathematical proofs to ensure that a model or algorithm satisfies certain predefined properties—such as safety, consistency, or bounded behavior. It offers strong guarantees of robustness under specified conditions. Though computationally expensive, it is increasingly applied to AI models in high-assurance domains.
Formal Verification Constraints
Formal verification constraints are the specific logical or mathematical conditions that a model must meet to be considered provably robust. These constraints may limit how much an input can change, restrict output ranges, or enforce invariant properties. They are central to certifiable robustness and safety-focused model design.
Fusion Engine
A fusion engine is a component in multimodal or agentic AI systems that integrates outputs from different sources—such as vision, text, or sensor data—into a unified understanding or decision. Its role is to synthesize information and guide action. If compromised, attackers can manipulate fusion weights or sequencing to distort the final behavior.
Generative Attention Vulnerability
Generative attention vulnerability refers to weaknesses in how attention mechanisms in generative models focus on input tokens or context. Adversaries can exploit these vulnerabilities to redirect focus toward irrelevant or malicious tokens, influencing outputs in subtle ways. This is a key risk area in large language models where attention patterns dictate response fidelity.
Gradient Alignment
Gradient alignment measures how well the direction of gradients—used in training or attack crafting—align with desired optimization goals. In adversarial contexts, attackers exploit this to ensure perturbations are maximally effective. Misaligned gradients can also indicate overfitting, noisy updates, or resistance to adversarial manipulation.
Gradient Anchoring
Gradient anchoring is a technique used in training where model updates are constrained to remain within a stable region of the parameter space. It's designed to reduce volatility and increase robustness against adversarial gradients. Anchoring can limit the risk of harmful model drift caused by poisoned or noisy updates.
Gradient Manipulation
Gradient manipulation is the act of altering the gradient signals used during training to inject backdoors, degrade accuracy, or cause misalignment. Attackers may use poisoned data or crafted updates in federated or collaborative learning settings. It is a stealthy and highly technical form of model poisoning.
Gradient Trojan Embedding
Gradient trojan embedding refers to embedding a backdoor into a model by manipulating its gradients during training so that it associates specific triggers with malicious behavior. This embedding is often invisible to evaluation metrics and lies dormant until the trigger is activated. It's a powerful method in white-box attack scenarios.
Gradient-Aligned Trojan
A gradient-aligned trojan is a backdoor designed to be highly effective during training by aligning its influence with the model's natural learning direction. These trojans avoid detection because they blend into the gradient dynamics of legitimate updates. They are particularly potent in federated learning and large-scale pretraining pipelines.
Gradient-Aware Auditing
Gradient-aware auditing is a technique used to analyze how gradients behave during training or fine-tuning to detect anomalies, poisoning, or backdoor signals. By monitoring gradients over time, defenders can flag subtle deviations in model learning. This approach offers insight into training-time manipulation beyond typical accuracy metrics.
Gradient-Based Evasion
Gradient-based evasion is an attack method that uses gradient information to craft inputs that are close to the decision boundary but still lead to misclassification. It is common in white-box attacks where the attacker can calculate or estimate gradients. These methods generate minimal, optimized perturbations that degrade model trustworthiness.
Gradient-Based Optimization
Gradient-based optimization is the core process behind training most machine learning models, where model weights are updated based on gradients that indicate the direction of improvement. Attackers also use this process to optimize perturbations or extract models. Securing gradient flows is critical for training integrity and adversarial defense.
Gradient-Based Perturbation
Gradient-based perturbation refers to the process of creating input changes—such as pixel adjustments or word substitutions—by following the gradient of a model's loss function. These perturbations are tailored to be effective while often remaining imperceptible. They are widely used in adversarial examples and model evasion attacks.
Hallucination Exploitation
Hallucination exploitation is the practice of deliberately triggering a generative model to produce false, misleading, or fabricated content in a way that benefits the attacker. This often involves crafted prompts that elicit confident but incorrect answers. It's a critical risk in systems that generate text, code, or images for high-stakes applications.
Homoglyph Substitution
Homoglyph substitution is an obfuscation technique where visually similar characters—such as replacing “o” with “0” or “l” with “1”—are used to deceive text-based AI models. These substitutions can bypass filters or mislead language models into interpreting malicious input as benign. It is widely used in adversarial text attacks and phishing-style prompts.
Illumination Manipulation
Illumination manipulation refers to altering lighting conditions in visual input—either in physical scenes or digital images—to degrade the performance of computer vision models. Adversaries may use shadows, glare, or color shifts to cause misclassification. It's a real-world tactic for defeating facial recognition, object detection, or surveillance systems.
Inference Activation
Inference activation describes the process of triggering specific behaviors or outputs in a model during the inference stage, often by presenting crafted inputs. This can include activating backdoors, prompting latent capabilities, or escalating decision logic. Attackers leverage inference activation to exploit models without access to training-time controls.
Inference API
An inference API is a web-accessible interface that allows users to submit inputs to a machine learning model and receive predictions or outputs. These APIs are common deployment endpoints but can be abused for probing, model extraction, or data leakage. Robust input validation and rate limiting are critical for API protection.
Inference Chaining
Inference chaining is a strategy where multiple AI model outputs are combined in sequence, with each step influencing the next. This chaining is common in multi-step reasoning and agentic pipelines. Attackers may exploit this to cause step-by-step degradation, compounding errors or injecting malicious influence that escalates with each inference.
Inference Drift
Inference drift refers to shifts in a model's predictions over time due to changes in input patterns, environmental signals, or internal state. Unlike training drift, inference drift occurs during use and may indicate environmental changes or adversarial activity. Monitoring output distributions helps detect unexpected drift in real-time systems.
Inference-Time Attack
An inference-time attack targets a model while it is running and making predictions, typically by feeding it crafted inputs designed to exploit its vulnerabilities. These attacks require no access to training data and are often used in real-world evasion scenarios. They are among the most common threats to deployed AI systems.
Inference-Time Exploitation
Inference-time exploitation encompasses any malicious action that takes place during a model's operational phase, including prompt injection, adversarial perturbation, or trigger activation. These attacks aim to subvert model output without modifying its internal parameters. This class of attack highlights the need for runtime safeguards.
Instruction Tuning
Instruction tuning is the process of training a generative model to follow natural language instructions, aligning it with specific task formats or conversational styles. While it improves usability, it can introduce new vulnerabilities if attackers manipulate how instructions are interpreted. Poor tuning can increase susceptibility to prompt-based attacks or hallucination.
Instruction-Following Fine-Tuning
Instruction-following fine-tuning is a specialized form of model adaptation where a model is trained on a dataset of prompt-response pairs that demonstrate desired behaviors in response to human-like instructions. While this improves compliance and usability, attackers can exploit ambiguities in instruction-following logic to induce unexpected or harmful behaviors.
Interval-Bound Propagation
Interval-bound propagation is a formal verification technique that tracks the upper and lower bounds of neural network outputs given bounded input changes. It is used to certify robustness against small perturbations. This method helps establish guarantees that no adversarial example can push the output past certain thresholds within defined limits.
Introspective Checkpoint
An introspective checkpoint is a saved model state that includes diagnostic information beyond just weights, such as gradient history, loss trajectories, or behavioral summaries. These enriched checkpoints aid in auditing, debugging, and anomaly detection. They also create opportunities to detect tampering or identify when a model's behavior began to drift.
Jailbreak
A jailbreak is a technique used to bypass the safety constraints of a generative model—particularly large language models—by crafting prompts that lead the model to produce restricted, harmful, or otherwise filtered outputs. Jailbreaking exposes the fragile boundaries between allowed and forbidden responses. It is one of the most widely observed attacks on public-facing AI.
Jailbreak Prompt
A jailbreak prompt is a specifically engineered input designed to coax a model into bypassing its content moderation or policy enforcement mechanisms. These prompts often use misdirection, multi-step context building, or role-playing to subvert guardrails. They are a primary tool for extracting unsafe or prohibited model outputs.
Latent Boundary Exploitation
Latent boundary exploitation is the act of crafting inputs that sit near the decision boundaries in the model's latent space to trigger ambiguous or incorrect outputs. By targeting the parts of latent space where representations are unstable, attackers can cause models to misbehave with seemingly valid inputs. It is particularly relevant in vision and generative models.
Latent Instruction
A latent instruction is an embedded directive hidden within input text or data that is not immediately visible to human reviewers but influences the model's output. This can take the form of prompt obfuscation, encoded commands, or context-based manipulation. Latent instructions are a form of covert prompt injection.
Latent Space Collision
Latent space collision occurs when two semantically different inputs are mapped to similar representations within a model's latent space. This can cause confusion in classification, generation, or reasoning tasks. Attackers can exploit collisions to craft adversarial inputs that evade detection or impersonate benign queries.
Latent Space Traversal
Latent space traversal is the process of moving through a model's internal representation space to explore or manipulate its behavior. This technique is used both for creative generation and adversarial control. Traversals can reveal sensitive or unstable zones in a model's reasoning pipeline.
Latent Trigger
A latent trigger is a pattern hidden within the input or internal model state that, once matched or activated, causes the model to behave in a predefined malicious way. These triggers are often introduced during training and remain dormant until activated in inference. They are central to backdoor and trojan attacks.
Layer-Targeted Poisoning
Layer-targeted poisoning is a form of model corruption in which poisoned data is crafted to affect specific internal layers of a neural network. Instead of altering output behavior directly, the attack changes how particular layers represent or process information. This can result in latent vulnerabilities that are only revealed under specific conditions or inputs.
Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is a technique used to explain model predictions by tracing how input features contribute to the final output across each layer of a network. It helps visualize which features are most influential and can uncover hidden biases or backdoors. LRP is a core tool in explainable AI and model auditing.
Lifecycle-Aware Threat Modeling
Lifecycle-aware threat modeling is the practice of assessing adversarial risks across all stages of an AI system's lifecycle—from data collection and training to deployment, monitoring, and decommissioning. This comprehensive view helps identify attack surfaces that change over time. It is essential for building resilient and trustworthy AI pipelines.
Linguistic Perturbation
Linguistic perturbation involves modifying natural language input—such as by changing synonyms, syntax, punctuation, or grammar—to deceive language models without altering semantic meaning. These changes are used to evade filters, confuse classifiers, or test model robustness. It is a common method in adversarial attacks on text-based systems.
Logic Bomb
A logic bomb is a hidden piece of code or condition embedded in a model that triggers malicious behavior when specific criteria are met. These are typically planted during training or fine-tuning and lie dormant until activated. Logic bombs are difficult to detect and pose a serious threat to AI supply chain integrity.
Logit Margin Check
Logit margin check refers to evaluating the difference between the top two logits—unnormalized output values of a model—to assess confidence and decision sharpness. Small margins may indicate uncertainty, adversarial influence, or label ambiguity. This check is used in robustness analysis and model auditing.
Low-Frequency Perturbation
Low-frequency perturbation is a visual attack technique where changes are made in smooth, broad patterns rather than pixel-level noise. These perturbations are harder to detect and can be more robust to compression, scaling, or environmental noise. They are effective in fooling image classifiers and detection models in real-world settings.
Membership Inference
Membership inference is a privacy attack where an adversary determines whether a specific data sample was included in a model's training set. This reveals potentially sensitive information and violates data protection principles. It is especially concerning for models trained on private or regulated datasets.
Memory Module
A memory module is a component within a machine learning system—often used in agentic or sequence-processing architectures—that stores and retrieves past observations, decisions, or interactions. If improperly secured, it can be manipulated to reinforce biased patterns or leak sensitive data. Attackers may target memory to induce long-term behavioral drift.
Memory Poisoning
Memory poisoning occurs when adversaries inject corrupted or malicious data into a model's memory module, influencing future predictions or decisions. This is particularly dangerous in systems that rely on retrieval-augmented generation or experience replay. Poisoned memory may persist long after the initial attack.
Memory Retrieval Vulnerability
Memory retrieval vulnerability refers to weaknesses in how an AI system accesses and ranks previously stored information from its internal or external memory. Attackers may exploit this by injecting misleading content into memory or manipulating query mechanisms to retrieve harmful or false entries. These vulnerabilities are particularly relevant in agentic systems and chatbots with long-term memory.
Memory Sanitization
Memory sanitization is the process of auditing, filtering, or clearing stored data from a model's memory to prevent the accumulation of harmful, sensitive, or adversarial content. This process is critical for maintaining trust in systems that learn from user interactions. Improper sanitization can leave residual exploits embedded in memory systems.
Metadata Spoofing
Metadata spoofing involves forging or manipulating metadata—such as timestamps, sources, authorship, or tags—to mislead models that rely on contextual or auxiliary data. It can be used to inject false authority, manipulate ranking algorithms, or misguide generative systems. It is a stealthy vector for influencing outputs without altering core content.
Model Alignment
Model alignment is the process of ensuring that an AI system's goals, behaviors, and outputs remain consistent with human intentions, values, and expectations. Alignment challenges arise when models generalize in unpredictable ways or misinterpret instructions. Misalignment can lead to unsafe actions, especially in high-autonomy or high-stakes settings.
Model Extraction
Model extraction is a type of attack where an adversary recreates a target model by querying it repeatedly and observing outputs. This reverse-engineering process can leak intellectual property or expose the model to further attacks. Even black-box models exposed through public APIs are vulnerable to extraction with enough queries.
Model Inversion
Model inversion is a privacy attack where adversaries use model outputs to reconstruct input features or entire records from the training data. This can reveal sensitive attributes such as medical details, images, or private identities. The attack exploits overfitting or memorization tendencies in the model.
Model Lineage
Model lineage tracks the ancestry and modification history of a model, including base checkpoints, fine-tuning stages, and data sources. Maintaining clear lineage is essential for auditing, reproducibility, and verifying model trust. Gaps in lineage records can mask the presence of inherited vulnerabilities or backdoors.
Model Poisoning
Model poisoning is the act of deliberately corrupting the training process—through poisoned data, gradients, or loss functions—to degrade performance or embed malicious behaviors. Unlike data poisoning, model poisoning can also involve modifying learning algorithms or injecting harmful logic directly. It is one of the most persistent and difficult-to-detect attack classes.
Model Reprogramming
Model reprogramming is an adversarial technique where an attacker uses crafted inputs to repurpose a model to perform an entirely different task than intended. This is often done without altering the model's architecture or weights. Reprogramming exploits the model's flexibility to perform tasks outside its original scope.
Model Supply Chain Contamination
Model supply chain contamination refers to the introduction of vulnerabilities—such as backdoors, bias, or poisoned data—during any phase of the model's creation, transfer, or deployment. This includes risks from pre-trained models, third-party libraries, or deployment infrastructure. It represents one of the most dangerous and least visible threats to trustworthy AI.
Model Versioning Exploit
A model versioning exploit targets weaknesses introduced through updates or changes to model versions over time. Attackers may test old and new versions for behavioral drift, vulnerabilities, or regressions that allow successful adversarial inputs. Improper change management can lead to inconsistent security guarantees across model releases.
Model Zoo
A model zoo is a collection or repository of pre-trained machine learning models, often shared for public use or fine-tuning. While convenient, these centralized hubs can introduce supply chain risks if models are not verified or curated. Malicious actors may upload contaminated models or exploit trust in popular downloads.
Multi-Modal Alignment
Multi-modal alignment refers to the process of ensuring that an AI system correctly integrates and interprets information from multiple data types—such as text, images, or audio. Poor alignment can lead to conflicting outputs or incoherent decisions. Attackers may exploit this misalignment to inject misleading content into one modality that affects overall reasoning.
Multi-Modal Evasion
Multi-modal evasion is an attack that manipulates one or more modalities to deceive a multi-modal system without being detected by others. For example, an adversarial image may be paired with a benign caption to bypass vision-language model filters. These attacks challenge assumptions that cross-modal models will self-correct.
Multi-Modal Fusion
Multi-modal fusion is the component of a model that integrates inputs from multiple modalities into a single unified representation. Attackers may target this fusion layer to misweight certain modalities or distort the output. Robust fusion design is essential for trustworthy decision-making in complex AI systems.
Multi-Modal Memorization
Multi-modal memorization occurs when an AI model inadvertently retains and recalls detailed training data across multiple input types. This can result in privacy violations or content leakage, particularly in generative systems that mix text and imagery. Detection is more difficult when memorization spans modalities.
Multi-Modal Perturbation
Multi-modal perturbation is the act of simultaneously modifying inputs across different modalities to achieve a desired adversarial effect. This synchronized manipulation can bypass modality-specific defenses and cause cascading model failures. These perturbations are particularly dangerous in models trained to process integrated media.
Multi-Model Ensemble Optimization
Multi-model ensemble optimization involves strategically combining multiple models to improve performance or robustness. However, attackers may poison one or more ensemble members to influence the overall output. Compromised ensembles can reduce interpretability and mask adversarial contributions from individual models.
Multi-Trigger Configuration
A multi-trigger configuration refers to the use of several different input triggers—either across modalities or time—that activate backdoor behaviors only when presented together. This makes detection harder and allows greater control over when and how malicious actions are initiated. It is a stealthy variant of conventional backdoor design.
Multi-Variate Time-Series
Multi-variate time-series data consist of multiple variables tracked over time and are common in forecasting, anomaly detection, and sensor systems. AI models that process such data are vulnerable to subtle manipulations that influence temporal trends or variable correlations. Attackers may target this structure to introduce delayed or compounding effects.
Observability
Observability refers to the degree to which the internal workings and states of a machine learning system can be understood from its external outputs and signals. High observability enables effective monitoring, debugging, and threat detection. In adversarial settings, low observability makes it harder to detect model compromise or behavioral drift.
Opaque Architecture
An opaque architecture is a model design that lacks transparency into its internal logic or component functions, often due to proprietary layers, black-box systems, or excessive complexity. This opacity hinders auditing, interpretability, and threat analysis. Attackers may exploit this lack of transparency to hide manipulations or persistent behaviors.
Output Filtering
Output filtering is the post-processing step that removes or blocks undesirable, unsafe, or policy-violating content from a model's response before it reaches the end user. While useful for content moderation, it is often bypassed by adversarial prompts or rephrasing. Filters may also introduce latency, hallucinations, or content distortion.
Output Sensitivity Threshold
An output sensitivity threshold defines the acceptable variance in model output in response to input perturbations. If the output changes too dramatically, it may indicate adversarial influence. Monitoring this threshold is critical for ensuring model robustness in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving or fraud detection.
Parameter Manipulation
Parameter manipulation is an adversarial technique that modifies the internal weights or hyperparameters of a model to embed backdoors, biases, or reduce accuracy. This can occur through unauthorized access or during compromised training and fine-tuning. Even subtle parameter changes can have outsized effects on behavior.
Parameter Perturbation
Parameter perturbation involves making slight changes to a model's internal parameters to test stability or induce misbehavior. Attackers may use this method to degrade performance without completely corrupting the model. It is also used in robustness testing to evaluate model sensitivity to internal noise.
Perturbation Attribution
Perturbation attribution is the process of tracing which specific changes in an input caused a shift in model output. It is used in adversarial forensics, debugging, and defense development. Effective attribution allows defenders to understand how adversarial examples succeed and how to patch the underlying vulnerability.
Perturbation Escalation
Perturbation escalation is a technique in which an attacker starts with small, undetectable changes and gradually increases perturbation magnitude over time to avoid detection. This strategy is effective in bypassing threshold-based defenses and achieving larger model influence without triggering alarms.
Perturbation Magnitude
Perturbation magnitude refers to the size or intensity of a change applied to input data in an adversarial attack. Smaller magnitudes are stealthier but harder to generate effectively, while larger ones are easier to spot. Measuring and constraining perturbation magnitude is key to certifying robustness.
Perturbation-Aware Gating
Perturbation-aware gating is a defensive mechanism that modulates model behavior based on the detection of potential adversarial perturbations. It may route inputs through hardened sub-models or apply filtering logic. This adaptive defense seeks to reduce the impact of adversarial examples without overreacting to benign variance.
Pixel-Level Perturbation
Pixel-level perturbation refers to the direct manipulation of individual pixels in an image input to deceive a computer vision model. These changes are often imperceptible to humans but can dramatically alter model predictions. It is one of the most common forms of adversarial evasion in image classification systems.
Plan Validator
A plan validator is a component used in agentic or decision-making AI systems that checks whether a proposed sequence of actions aligns with predefined rules, goals, or constraints. If compromised, attackers can insert malicious plans that pass validation or suppress legitimate ones. Validators are critical in autonomous and safety-sensitive systems.
Poisoned Data
Poisoned data consists of input examples intentionally modified to manipulate a model's learning process. This data may appear benign but contains hidden patterns or triggers that degrade performance or embed vulnerabilities. Poisoning is a foundational tactic in adversarial machine learning, particularly during model training or fine-tuning.
Poisoned Embedding
A poisoned embedding is a vector representation that has been subtly altered to introduce vulnerabilities or mislead downstream models. Because embeddings are reused across systems, poisoned versions can propagate errors, biases, or backdoors silently. These attacks often target shared NLP or vision embedding spaces.
Poisoning Attack
A poisoning attack is a strategy where an adversary injects manipulated training data to control or degrade a model's performance. This may be done to cause misclassifications, embed triggers, or create unfair outputs. Poisoning is one of the most difficult attack types to detect, especially in open-data pipelines.
Policy Brittleness
Policy brittleness describes a model's tendency to fail or behave erratically when exposed to inputs that are slightly outside its training distribution or operational context. This fragility can be exploited by adversaries to induce policy violations or unexpected behavior. It highlights the importance of stress testing decision policies.
Policy Distillation
Policy distillation is the process of transferring decision-making knowledge from one model (usually larger or more complex) into a smaller, faster model. While useful for deployment efficiency, it may carry over hidden biases or vulnerabilities. Attackers can exploit this to preserve or smuggle adversarial traits into lightweight models.
Positional Encoding
Positional encoding is a technique used in transformer models to represent the order of input tokens, since these architectures lack inherent sequence awareness. By encoding token positions into embeddings, models can understand context and structure. Adversaries may exploit weaknesses in this encoding to shift meaning or induce hallucinations.
Prefix Manipulation
Prefix manipulation involves modifying or inserting content at the beginning of an input prompt to influence or control a generative model's output. This is a common tactic in prompt injection, where the attacker adds misleading or malicious context to guide model behavior. It can override safety instructions or redirect intent.
Progressive Framing Injection
Progressive framing injection is an adversarial method where malicious instructions are introduced gradually across a conversation or document. This slow buildup avoids triggering safety mechanisms and allows attackers to shift the model's behavior incrementally. It is particularly effective in chat-based and multi-turn interaction settings.
Prompt Conditioning
Prompt conditioning refers to the practice of shaping a model's behavior by carefully designing the initial prompt or system message. It sets the tone, constraints, or assumptions for all downstream responses. Attackers may subvert this mechanism by injecting contradictory or misleading context to bypass safety or alignment goals.
Prompt Injection
Prompt injection is an adversarial technique where malicious instructions are embedded in a user input or external source to hijack the behavior of a language model. This can override intended constraints, force model compliance, or extract hidden functions. It is one of the most prevalent attacks in generative AI systems.
Prompt Injection Extraction
Prompt injection extraction is the act of using prompt injection techniques to reveal internal instructions, prompt templates, or system-level behaviors that are supposed to be hidden from users. These attacks compromise confidentiality and can expose sensitive or proprietary prompt engineering.
Prompt Stress Testing
Prompt stress testing is a red-teaming technique that systematically challenges a model's prompt handling abilities with adversarial, ambiguous, or conflicting inputs. It helps identify weaknesses in instruction-following, safety adherence, and robustness. It is essential for evaluating model alignment and jailbreak resilience.
Prompt-Based Extraction
Prompt-based extraction is a technique used to elicit hidden knowledge or training data from a model by carefully crafting input prompts. These prompts guide the model to recall memorized data or repeat patterns from pretraining. It is a major concern in privacy-sensitive applications.
Provenance Tracking
Provenance tracking refers to documenting the origin, handling, and transformation of data or model outputs throughout the AI pipeline. It supports transparency, accountability, and tamper detection. In adversarial settings, attackers may try to spoof or erase provenance to hide their influence.
Reasoning Trajectory
A reasoning trajectory is the internal path a model takes as it processes inputs and generates outputs, often represented by intermediate steps or latent states. Understanding these trajectories can help explain model behavior and detect manipulations. Adversaries may attempt to redirect or corrupt this reasoning path.
Recursive Reasoning
Recursive reasoning is a strategy where a model repeatedly evaluates or refines its own outputs to improve coherence, accuracy, or multi-step logic. While useful in complex tasks, this recursion can be hijacked to reinforce incorrect assumptions or amplify adversarial inputs across iterations.
Recursive Reasoning Loop
A recursive reasoning loop is a self-referential decision-making process in which a model continuously reprocesses its outputs as new inputs. If not properly bounded, this can lead to instability, hallucinations, or compounding errors. Attackers may exploit this loop to escalate influence or trigger infinite feedback.
Red-Teaming
Red-teaming is a structured adversarial evaluation process where models are tested against intentionally harmful or manipulative inputs to uncover vulnerabilities. It is an essential practice for assessing robustness, safety, and policy adherence. Red-teaming helps identify flaws before real-world deployment.
Reinforced Reprogramming
Reinforced reprogramming involves adapting a model to perform unintended tasks using reinforcement learning methods—typically without changing its core architecture. Attackers use this to embed alternate goals into otherwise aligned models. It poses a major risk when access to the reward function or training pipeline is exposed.
Relevance Redistribution
Relevance redistribution refers to shifting a model's attention or importance weights away from relevant features and toward misleading or irrelevant ones. This undermines interpretability and can cause misclassification or poor decision-making. Adversaries often exploit this during feature attribution attacks.
Representation Centroid Shift
Representation centroid shift occurs when the average internal embedding of a class or concept drifts due to adversarial fine-tuning, poisoning, or continual learning. This shift can degrade accuracy, cause overlap between distinct concepts, or enable misclassification. Monitoring centroid stability is important for model integrity.
Representation Hijacking
Representation hijacking is the adversarial takeover of a model's internal representations, redirecting them to encode attacker-controlled semantics. This affects how the model understands inputs and can lead to covert backdoor activation or semantic confusion. It's a stealthy and deeply embedded form of model manipulation.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines a generative model with a retrieval component that fetches external documents or facts to support output generation. While powerful, RAG systems are vulnerable to poisoning in the retrieval source, prompt injection in documents, or misalignment between facts and generation.
Reward Shaping
Reward shaping is the practice of modifying a reinforcement learning reward signal to guide model behavior more effectively or encourage alignment with desired outcomes. If done improperly—or adversarially—it can introduce unintended incentives or reinforce harmful patterns.
Reward-Shaping Attack
A reward-shaping attack occurs when an attacker manipulates the reward function or feedback process of a reinforcement learning system to encourage undesirable or harmful behavior. This may lead to misaligned learning, goal divergence, or reward hacking. It poses a serious threat to agentic systems with online learning.
Robust Accuracy
Robust accuracy measures how well a model performs under adversarial conditions or input perturbations. Unlike standard accuracy, it evaluates performance in the presence of attacks or noise. High robust accuracy is a key indicator of resilience in safety-critical applications.
RobustBench
RobustBench is a standardized benchmark and leaderboard for evaluating the adversarial robustness of machine learning models. It includes curated datasets, evaluation metrics, and attack scenarios. It helps researchers and practitioners compare defenses and track progress in adversarial machine learning.
Role Reframing
Role reframing is a prompt injection technique where an attacker changes the perceived identity or context of the model—such as making it believe it is a fictional character, alternate persona, or different system. This can trick the model into bypassing rules or generating otherwise restricted content.
Roleplay Exploit
A roleplay exploit manipulates a language model by framing prompts as fictional or hypothetical scenarios, which can lead the model to bypass safety filters and generate restricted content. By pretending the model is playing a character, attackers can sidestep alignment mechanisms and invoke otherwise disallowed behaviors.
Runtime Anomaly Detection
Runtime anomaly detection is the process of monitoring a model's behavior during inference to identify deviations from expected norms. It includes detecting abnormal outputs, API usage, or execution patterns. This form of defense is critical for real-time systems that must respond to evolving adversarial threats.
Saliency Map Divergence
Saliency map divergence occurs when visualizations of model attention or feature importance differ significantly across similar inputs. This divergence can indicate instability, adversarial manipulation, or hidden biases. Tracking saliency consistency helps detect subtle attacks and evaluate explanation reliability.
Security Debt
Security debt refers to the accumulation of unresolved security risks, vulnerabilities, or weak assumptions in AI systems over time. As models evolve or become more integrated, unaddressed security gaps can compound and become harder to manage. Recognizing and reducing security debt is vital for long-term system safety.
Semantic Ambiguity Injection
Semantic ambiguity injection involves crafting inputs that exploit multiple interpretations or unclear meanings to mislead AI models. These inputs may appear legitimate but result in unpredictable or harmful outputs. It is a common tactic in language models, especially in bypassing safety filters or triggering edge-case behaviors.
Semantic Boundary Exploitation
Semantic boundary exploitation targets the fine line between similar concepts in a model's latent or classification space. Adversaries craft inputs that hover near these boundaries, causing the model to flip between interpretations or classifications. This reveals the fragility of semantic decision-making in AI systems.
Semantic Collision
Semantic collision occurs when different inputs map to similar internal representations despite having different meanings. This can lead to misclassification, confusion, or blending of concepts in generative systems. Attackers may intentionally create collisions to inject malicious content masked as benign.
Semantic Drift
Semantic drift refers to the gradual shift in how a model understands or interprets language or concepts over time. This may occur due to new data, fine-tuning, or environmental changes. Adversaries may exploit drift to reintroduce deprecated or harmful behaviors that the model had previously unlearned.
Semantic Misalignment
Semantic misalignment happens when a model's interpretation of input diverges from the user's intended meaning. This disconnect can lead to inaccurate predictions or dangerous outputs. It is a core risk in natural language processing and instruction-following systems, particularly under adversarial influence.
Semantic Parsing
Semantic parsing is the process of converting natural language into structured representations, such as logical forms or command sequences. It enables models to interface with databases, APIs, or tools. Attackers may manipulate inputs to trick the parser into producing harmful or unintended interpretations.
Semantic Perturbation
Semantic perturbation involves altering input text in ways that preserve its overall meaning while changing its form, with the goal of misleading a model. This may include rephrasing, using synonyms, or adjusting grammar. It is a common method for bypassing content filters or evading classification systems.
Semantic Proximity
Semantic proximity refers to how closely two concepts or inputs are related within a model's latent or embedding space. High proximity suggests the model considers them similar, which can influence classification or generation. Adversaries may exploit this by crafting inputs that appear harmless but fall near dangerous concepts.
Semantic Segmentation Evasion
Semantic segmentation evasion targets models that classify each pixel in an image according to its object class. Attackers modify inputs to cause segmentation errors, such as hiding objects or misclassifying backgrounds. This is particularly critical in autonomous vehicles and medical imaging, where pixel-level precision is vital.
Sequential Drift
Sequential drift is a gradual change in model predictions over time within a single session or task sequence, often caused by accumulated errors or adversarial inputs. This drift may not be immediately detectable but can degrade output quality or alignment. It is particularly relevant in dialogue systems and long-form generation.
Sequential Reasoning
Sequential reasoning refers to a model's ability to carry out multi-step logic or inference, where each step builds on the previous one. Adversaries may target this process by introducing misleading inputs early in the sequence to bias the outcome. Robust sequential reasoning is essential for mathematical problem solving, planning, and agentic behavior.
Session Carryover
Session carryover is the persistence of context or memory across user interactions in multi-turn systems. While useful for continuity, it can be exploited if adversaries inject harmful context that influences future outputs. Managing and sanitizing session memory is critical in persistent AI assistants.
Session Memory Poisoning
Session memory poisoning is a specific attack where an adversary intentionally inserts malicious or misleading information into a model's session memory. This poisoned memory can affect future outputs or reasoning, even if the attacker is no longer interacting with the system. It is a growing concern in models with long-term conversational memory.
Softmax Attention
Softmax attention is a mechanism used in transformer models to weigh input tokens during processing, using a softmax function to assign relative importance. It determines what the model “pays attention” to at each layer. Manipulating attention weights through adversarial inputs can redirect model focus and cause misinterpretation.
Spectral Normalization
Spectral normalization is a technique that constrains the Lipschitz constant of a neural network by controlling the spectral norm of weight matrices. It helps stabilize training and improve robustness against adversarial perturbations. It is commonly used in generative adversarial networks and certified defenses.
Spike Damping
Spike damping is a defensive method used to suppress extreme activations or output fluctuations in neural networks. By reducing sudden spikes, models become less sensitive to small input perturbations. This technique helps mitigate the effects of gradient-based adversarial attacks that rely on inducing sharp output changes.
State-Based Exploit
A state-based exploit targets an AI system's internal or environmental state—such as memory, variables, or configuration—to influence its behavior. These attacks often involve manipulating system flags, history, or execution flow to bypass intended logic. They are particularly effective in agentic or decision-based architectures.
Statistical Perturbation
Statistical perturbation involves altering input data distributions—such as means, variances, or correlations—to shift model behavior without triggering individual anomalies. This technique is used to induce silent drift, bias outputs, or degrade performance across large populations. It is commonly seen in data poisoning at scale.
Subdomain Hijacking
Subdomain hijacking occurs when an attacker takes control of a previously valid but now-unused subdomain referenced by an AI model—often in training data, links, or tools. This enables the attacker to serve malicious content that the model retrieves or embeds. It is a subtle but dangerous threat in retrieval-augmented and tool-using systems.
Subtask Corruption
Subtask corruption is an attack that targets specific components or steps in a larger task pipeline, such as planning, classification, or data retrieval. By compromising one part of a multi-stage system, adversaries can distort the final output while avoiding detection at the overall task level.
Supply Chain Attack
A supply chain attack on AI targets any upstream component—such as training data, libraries, pre-trained models, or infrastructure—used to build or run a model. These attacks inject vulnerabilities before deployment, often hidden in dependencies or third-party tools. They are among the most difficult to detect and mitigate.
Surrogate Model
A surrogate model is an approximate copy of a target model used by attackers to test or craft adversarial examples. It mimics the behavior of the original system, especially when the target is black-box. High transferability between surrogate and target models increases the effectiveness of black-box attacks.
Sybil Attack
A Sybil attack involves an adversary creating multiple fake identities—such as user accounts, clients, or contributors—to influence a distributed system. In federated learning or crowdsourced AI, Sybil nodes can poison updates, skew voting, or introduce coordinated bias. Detecting Sybil behavior is crucial in decentralized model governance.
Symbolic Reasoning Module
A symbolic reasoning module is a component that uses rule-based logic, rather than neural approximations, to process structured data or enforce constraints. These modules improve interpretability and trust but may be targeted by adversaries through constraint violations, edge-case logic, or input misrepresentation.
System Prompt Override
System prompt override is a prompt injection technique that bypasses a language model's initial instruction or policy prompt—often hidden from the user—by providing conflicting or higher-priority instructions. Attackers exploit this to hijack model alignment and force unauthorized responses.
Systemic Trust
Systemic trust refers to the degree to which users, institutions, or environments rely on AI systems across multiple layers—such as infrastructure, social interaction, or automation. Breaches of this trust can cascade across applications and amplify risk. Adversarial threats that affect foundational components may erode systemic trust quickly and broadly.
Telemetry Spoofing
Telemetry spoofing is the manipulation or falsification of monitoring data sent from an AI system to observers, dashboards, or automated defenses. Attackers may alter logs, performance metrics, or usage statistics to hide adversarial activity, evade detection, or simulate compliance. Robust telemetry verification is essential for trust and traceability.
Temporal Poisoning
Temporal poisoning is an attack strategy that introduces harmful data or triggers over time, gradually influencing a model's behavior without immediate detection. This slow-burn poisoning is particularly effective in continual learning and streaming contexts, where historical data plays a significant role in shaping future outputs.
Threat Taxonomy
A threat taxonomy is a structured framework that categorizes types of adversarial attacks, vulnerabilities, and risk factors in AI systems. It provides a common vocabulary and helps defenders prioritize mitigations. Taxonomies often distinguish between training-time vs. inference-time threats, or evasion vs. poisoning.
Token Completion Patterns
Token completion patterns refer to the statistical or semantic patterns a language model learns when predicting the next token. Attackers can exploit these patterns to guide or control output in subtle ways. Understanding and stress-testing these completions is crucial for hardening generative models against manipulation.
Tokenization Artifact
A tokenization artifact is an unintended consequence of how input text is split into tokens—often due to model-specific encoding rules—that can affect meaning, representation, or prediction. These artifacts can be exploited to evade filters, inject hidden content, or cause semantic distortion in language processing tasks.
Token-Level Attribution
Token-level attribution refers to techniques that assign importance scores to individual tokens based on their contribution to a model's output. It is widely used in interpretability and auditing. Attackers may exploit attribution mechanisms to hide harmful inputs or mislead human reviewers.
Token-Level Perturbation
Token-level perturbation is a method of altering individual words or subwords in text to change model behavior while preserving semantics. It is often used in adversarial NLP attacks, especially to test robustness of classification and generation systems. These perturbations can be designed to evade filters or redirect attention.
Tool Interface Policy
A tool interface policy defines the rules and constraints under which a model can invoke external tools, APIs, or functions. Weak or misconfigured policies can allow unintended access, misuse, or privilege escalation. This is a critical aspect of securing agentic AI systems with tool-using capabilities.
Tool Invocation Interface
The tool invocation interface is the component through which an AI system interacts with external utilities, such as search engines, calculators, or file systems. Attackers may exploit this interface to trigger harmful tool usage, redirect outputs, or leak sensitive information. Validation and access control are essential safeguards.
Tool Misuse
Tool misuse refers to scenarios where a model invokes an external function or utility in a harmful, unintended, or policy-violating way—either due to adversarial prompting or internal error. This can result in data leakage, system compromise, or real-world harm. Preventing tool misuse is key to safe AI deployment.
Transfer Learning Propagation
Transfer learning propagation refers to the phenomenon where vulnerabilities, biases, or adversarial behaviors learned in a source model are inherited by downstream models through fine-tuning or re-use. This propagation can silently transmit risk across model families, especially in open model ecosystems.
Transfer Poisoning
Transfer poisoning is an attack where poisoned data is introduced into a model used for transfer learning, embedding vulnerabilities that survive during fine-tuning. These attacks target general-purpose pre-trained models, compromising entire downstream pipelines even when the target data is clean.
Transfer Robustness Testing
Transfer robustness testing evaluates how well a model maintains accuracy and security when adversarial examples or poisoned data are transferred from another model. This type of testing is critical for assessing generalization of defenses across architectures or deployment environments.
Transferability
Transferability describes how easily adversarial examples created for one model can affect another model, even with different architectures or training data. High transferability enables black-box attacks and exposes systemic weaknesses in model families that share similar decision boundaries.
Transferability Score
A transferability score quantifies how effectively an adversarial input generated for one model can be used to deceive another. This score helps compare model robustness and identify attack surfaces shared across multiple systems.
Transferable Perturbation
A transferable perturbation is a crafted input modification that reliably deceives multiple models across tasks or architectures. These perturbations are designed to exploit common features or weaknesses in learning processes. Their existence challenges the effectiveness of model-specific defenses.
Transformer Gradient Dynamics
Transformer gradient dynamics refers to the behavior of gradient flows within transformer architectures during training or adversarial optimization. Understanding these dynamics helps researchers identify instability, vulnerability, and opportunities for robust training or attack resistance.
Trigger Activation Path
A trigger activation path is the internal computational pathway through which a backdoor or trojan trigger causes a model to switch behaviors. Mapping this path helps defenders locate where malicious logic is embedded and how it flows through the network.
Trigger Collisions
Trigger collisions occur when multiple backdoor triggers unintentionally activate the same or conflicting malicious behaviors within a model. These collisions can degrade attack precision or cause unintended outputs, and they present a potential opportunity for detection.
Trigger Embedding
Trigger embedding is the insertion of a backdoor signal into the internal representation space of a model, often in a way that survives pruning, fine-tuning, or distributional shift. These embeddings are designed to remain dormant until the attacker presents the matching input pattern.
Trigger-Response Behavior
Trigger-response behavior describes the hidden logic programmed into a model where a specific input (the trigger) causes a pre-defined, often harmful or attacker-controlled, output. This behavior is central to backdoor and trojan attacks and is usually imperceptible during standard testing.
Trojan Model Artifact
A trojan model artifact is a file, checkpoint, or component that contains a model with embedded backdoors, poisoned weights, or malicious logic. These artifacts are often distributed through public model repositories or compromised supply chains and can compromise downstream applications if used blindly.
Vulnerability Map
A vulnerability map is a diagnostic tool or visualization that highlights regions in input or latent space where a model is most susceptible to adversarial manipulation. It helps researchers and defenders understand risk surfaces, optimize testing, and design more robust systems.
White-Box Attack
A white-box attack is a threat model in which the attacker has full access to the model's architecture, parameters, and training data. This enables highly optimized adversarial inputs, backdoor insertion, or gradient-based evasion. White-box attacks represent the strongest form of adversarial threat.
